one_liner: Single-header C library for embedding a non-blocking HTTP/1.1 server; the author's 2019 ab hello-world run beat a one-worker nginx 1.14 by about 1.7x.
what_it_does: Lets a C or C++ program serve HTTP/1.1 from one header: define HTTPSERVER_IMPL in one file, call http_server_init(port, handler) and http_server_listen(), and build each reply in the callback with http_response_status/header/body plus http_respond. Large or chunked request bodies are streamed with http_request_read_chunk, chunked responses go out with http_respond_chunk, and a poll mode (http_server_listen_poll plus http_server_poll) fits programs that already run their own update loop, such as games. It is a library you embed, not a configurable server: there is no static-file serving, routing, proxying, TLS or HTTP/2.
how_it_is_fast: One thread runs an edge-triggered epoll (Linux) or kqueue (BSD, macOS) loop over non-blocking sockets. A Ragel-generated state-machine parser records each request element as an (offset, length) token into the read buffer, so request strings are zero-copy slices, and the Date header is cached and refreshed by a one-second timer. Each response is serialized into one buffer and sent with a single write(). Nothing exotic is involved (no io_uring, writev batching or SIMD): epoll_wait takes one event per call, every connection gets its own timerfd, and a request costs several malloc/free pairs, so the win over nginx comes from doing very little per request rather than from a special technique.
when_to_use: Adding a small HTTP endpoint (health check, metrics, local REST control API, debug console) to an existing C or C++ program on Linux, FreeBSD or macOS, with no dependencies beyond POSIX sockets.

Single-threaded programs that already own a main loop: poll mode handles at most one ready request per http_server_poll call, and http_server_loop exposes the epoll/kqueue descriptor so your own fds can share it.
Small replies on keep-alive connections from a trusted client or behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS and HTTP/2, which is the only workload the published numbers cover.
When you want an MIT-licensed single file you can vendor and patch, and you will keep response headers under about 1 KB (see gotchas).
when_not_to_use: Internet-facing without a hardened proxy in front: the response-header overflow bug below is still on master, issue #77 (signed overflow when parsing Content-Length, filed 2026-05-29) and #72 (keep-alive mis-parsing) are open with no maintainer reply, and there is no TLS.
Windows (issue #63, no support) or any platform without epoll or kqueue.
Multi-core throughput: there is one event-loop thread and no worker model; the listening socket sets SO_REUSEPORT, so scaling means running several processes yourself.

Clients that pipeline HTTP/1.1 requests (wrk pipelining scripts, TechEmpower plaintext): bytes of a second request read together with the first are freed when http_respond swaps the request buffer for the response buffer, so that request is never answered and the connection idles until the 120 s keep-alive timeout.
Tens of thousands of idle keep-alive connections: on Linux every connection owns a timerfd that wakes the loop once a second, and keep-alive connections are held for 120 s by default.

integration.form: header-only (single generated header; #define HTTPSERVER_IMPL in exactly one .c or .cpp file); src/ also builds a CMake static library libhttpsrv, which needs ragel and m4 to regenerate the parser and header
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (POSIX sockets; epoll and timerfd on Linux, kqueue on BSD and macOS); ragel and m4 only when rebuilding from src/
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (CMake sets C_STANDARD 99); usable from C++ through extern "C" (the functional tests have a C++ mode); specific compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll) and FreeBSD, OpenBSD and macOS (kqueue); no Windows. The single header does not auto-detect the platform: compile with -DEPOLL on Linux or -DKQUEUE on BSD and macOS (only the CMake build detects this).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; everything runs on one event-loop thread with no locking, so call the API only from that thread

gotchas: Response-header serialization bug (src/respond.c _grwprintf, still on master after the 2026-04-26 va_list fix d095bae): when the headers outgrow the 1024-byte HTTP_RESPONSE_BUF_SIZE, the retry does `bytes += vsnprintf(...)`, counting the overflowing header line twice, so the response carries that many uninitialized heap bytes; if the doubled size passes the new capacity, the next vsnprintf gets a negative length converted to a huge size_t and writes past the buffer. The `>` check is also off by one, so a line that exactly fills the buffer loses its last byte to the NUL. Keep total response headers well under 1 KB or patch it to `bytes = vsnprintf(...)` with a `>=` test. The hello-world benchmark sends about 130 bytes, so this bug sits outside the numbers.

Keep-alive connections never reset their token array (tokens.size is zeroed only at accept), so http_request_target, http_request_header and the keep-alive check return the first request's offsets applied to the current buffer. A later request with a different-length URL or header layout is mis-read (issue #72, open since 2024-02, no maintainer reply), and the array grows with every request on the connection. The ab -k benchmark repeats one identical request about 500 times per connection with a handler that reads nothing from the request, so it cannot show this bug.

Benchmark harness flaws: the nginx config in the README cannot be loaded as written (it has no events block, which nginx requires), so the actual file is unknown. It leaves access logging on and keepalive_requests at its default (99,052 of 100,000 keep-alive), and its add_header Content-Type on top of nginx's default_type likely sends two Content-Type headers (about 210 vs 134 bytes per response, derived from page data). Both nginx runs show 1 s connect outliers (max 1029 and 1123 ms) that httpserver.h never hit. The single-threaded ab client at ~124k req/s may itself have been the limit.

Request strings (http_string_s) are not NUL-terminated and stay valid only until http_respond, which frees the request buffer. hs_write_socket tests a stale errno == EPIPE without checking write()'s return, so a leftover EPIPE can close a connection whose write succeeded. Content-Length parsing overflows int64 on huge values (#77). The documented HTTP_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH (8 KB) is not what the Ragel parser enforces: src/parser.rl hard-codes 1024 bytes for the request target, 256 for header names and 4096 for header values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick httpserver.h over libuhttpd, Lwan, Kore or H2O when you want one MIT header with no dependencies inside an existing C or C++ program and can live with one thread and HTTP/1.1 only. Those siblings are full servers or frameworks with stronger evidence against nginx (wrk runs, TechEmpower) and multi-core designs, so they are the better choice when throughput or exposure to untrusted clients matters.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran ApacheBench on localhost in December 2019 (ab -c 200 -n 100000, 13-byte Hello, World! body) against nginx 1.14.0 with worker_processes 1: 123,908 vs 74,441 req/s with keep-alive (about 1.66x) and 27,605 vs 15,773 req/s with Connection: close (about 1.75x). No CPU, OS, compiler or flags are given, the server binary came from the 2019 code rather than today's src/ tree, and the author says the run was a reference point, not a claim of superiority.
status_note: Dormant from 2023 until a burst of fixes and fuzzing on 2026-04-25/26 (socket leak, va_list reuse), but the response-header overflow above is still on master and keep-alive mis-parsing (#72) and Content-Length overflow (#77) are open without maintainer replies. It is MIT-licensed and one file, so vendor it and patch those bugs before exposing it to untrusted clients.
